newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Aust-NZ investment, tax issues loom large -council.
newsitem.headline: Aust-NZ investment, tax issues loom large -council.

text.p: The Australia-New Zealand business council on Friday praised progress in trans-Tasman economic relations but said significant issues remain on the agenda.

New Zealand council chairman Kerry McDonald, speaking ahead of a three-day conference on Ausrtalian and New Zealand business competitiveness, told a briefing of journalists that the process of developing trade relations had come a long way under the Closer Economic Relations (CER) agreement.
"So we do tend to talk now about the unfinished business, which is still pretty significant," he said. Top of the list of issues were rules of origin, investment and tax.
"Rules or origin; the problem is the 50 percent domestic content requirement," McDonald said.

"Australia has been very reluctant at the official level to make progress on that. They're saying this is a multilateral issue and must be dealt with in terms of multilateral processes that are already under way.
"Now both the Australian and New Zealand business communities are saying 'no', it's an issue that should be dealt with more quickly, even if it's on an interim basis."
McDonald said there was also negative sentiment surrounding tax issues.

"It's not credible to talk in terms of a common tax system for Australia and New Zealand, but it's things like the transfer of franking credits -- that is the critical issue," he said. "If you've got cross-border investment, then it's silly to have non-transferability of franking credits."
He said work was being done to look at the the tax treatment of foreign investors, who were currently "quite clearly disadvantaged."

There were, for example, offshore shareholders in New Zealand companies whose earnings had to come back into New Zealand, go through the New Zealand tax system, and then go back into their own home-base tax system. "It's a major disincentive to invest in New Zealand," McDonald said.
There was now a very high volume of investment between Australia and New Zealand and the council was keen to see an umbrella framework agreement put in place.

"There's a double tax agreement, which is a key document, but it's limited in it's scope, and there's no obligation on either side to maintain a particular standard of behaviour in relation to those cross-border investments," McDonald said.

"So we are very keen to see some sort of framework agreement in place. Obviously the end result is that we want...New Zealand investment to be treated in Austrlia as if it were domestic investment, and the same coming the other way."
He said there had already been some discussion on the question of an investment agreement between the two countries.
"My understanding is that discussions have to go some way yet before it's clear that there is a basis for an agreement.

"The important thing is that between (New Zealand Finance Minister) Bill Birch and (Australian Treasurer) Peter Costello, there is now some meeting of the minds on seeing what can be done in this area."

McDonald said the change of government in Australia had brought a "new view, vision, willingness to discuss issues", but added: "Perhaps it's unfortunate that the bureaucracy in Canberra doesn't completely change at the same time as the government does, because there are still, we perceive, pockets
...that are pretty resistant on a number of key issues."

The three-day conference in Auckland, starting on September 25, would look at the question of competitiveness: how the two countries had done over the last 10 or 20 years, how they were positioned now, and what their future prospects were.
"The whole purpose of CER is to make Australia and New Zealand more competitive with the rest of the world, not just to improve trade between the two countries," McDonald said.
--Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
